note: The deceptive-pattern catalog as DATA, not prose. It is allowed to grow without bound because nobody reads it whole: a founder sees only the rows for the surfaces their product actually has. Prose judgment (effect-not-intent, symmetry-in-choice, humane defaults, the record-the-crossing mechanism) lives in library/practices/deceptive-patterns.md and is NOT duplicated here. Consumers: `boss craft deceptive-patterns [--shape X] [--surface Y]`, /red-team --humane, /ux-check, /trust, the deception conscience moment, and scripts/check-pattern-coverage.js. MINORS IS A MODIFIER, NOT A SURFACE (decided 2026-08-21): every other surface is a PLACE in the product, while "minors" is a property of the USER — so it never had a coherent home and sat at 2 rows. Rows now carry an optional stricter_when_minors (same pattern, higher bar), and `boss craft deceptive-patterns --minors` lists every row that has one.

dev-tool.label: Library, SDK, API, or developer platform

marketing-site.label: Landing page, waitlist, or content site

agent.label: Agent that acts on the user's behalf

marketplace.label: Two-sided platform that matches, ranks, or pays people

ecommerce.label: Sells goods or subscriptions; has a cart

health-or-regulated.label: Health, legal, financial, or other high-stakes domain

hardware-or-iot.label: Physical device, sensor, or location product

signup-and-identity.label: Signup & identity
signup-and-identity.detect: Is there an account, a login, an email capture, or an OAuth grant?

consent-ui.label: The consent surface
consent-ui.detect: Is there a cookie banner, a consent dialog, or a privacy toggle anywhere?
consent-ui.note: Visible. /ux-check can read this one — button weight, default state, what the copy says.

tracking-and-telemetry.label: Tracking & telemetry
tracking-and-telemetry.detect: Do you send anything about a user to a third party — analytics, ads, a pixel, an SDK, a model provider?
tracking-and-telemetry.note: The pattern family with almost NO UI. There is nothing to look at, which is why /ux-check cannot catch it and /trust must.

checkout-and-pricing.label: Checkout & pricing
checkout-and-pricing.detect: Does anyone pay you, at any point, for anything?

cancel-and-delete.label: Cancel, export & delete
cancel-and-delete.detect: Can someone leave — end a subscription, close an account, take their data out?

notifications-and-engagement.label: Notifications & engagement
notifications-and-engagement.detect: Does the product try to bring someone back — push, email, streaks, reminders?

social-proof-and-claims.label: Social proof & claims
social-proof-and-claims.detect: Does the product make claims about itself — reviews, testimonials, user counts, capabilities, benchmarks?

ai-voice.label: The AI's own voice
ai-voice.detect: Does a model talk to the user in its own voice?

agent-actions.label: Agent actions
agent-actions.detect: Does something act on the user's behalf without them watching each step?

generated-markup.label: The markup the model wrote
generated-markup.detect: Did an AI write any of the UI you shipped?
generated-markup.note: The keystone surface for BOSS: the founder did not design these and often cannot see them.

device-permissions.label: Device permissions
device-permissions.detect: Does the product ask the OS for camera, mic, location, contacts, photos, or notifications?

install-and-update.label: Install, update & deprecation
install-and-update.detect: Does someone install this, and do you ship updates to it?

metering-and-credits.label: Metering & credits
metering-and-credits.detect: Is anything priced by usage — tokens, credits, calls, seats-by-activity?

scoring-and-pay.label: Scoring, ranking & pay
scoring-and-pay.detect: Does the product score, rank, match, or pay a person?

bystanders.label: Bystanders
bystanders.detect: Do you hold data about people who are not users and never agreed to anything?
bystanders.note: The axis neither harm framework carries. Added 2026-08-20.

content-and-moderation.label: Content & moderation
content-and-moderation.detect: Can one user's content reach another user?

patterns.name: Accept prominent, Reject buried
patterns.looks_like: "Accept All" is a solid coloured button; declining is a grey text link, a second screen, or absent entirely.
patterns.honest: Reject is one click, the same weight, on the same screen. If the good door takes more clicks than the bad one, you have already failed.

patterns.name: Trackers fire before the click
patterns.looks_like: The banner renders, but the analytics and ad tags already loaded. The choice is decorative.
patterns.honest: Nothing non-essential loads until consent is given. Test it with the network tab, not the code.
patterns.teeth: GDPR / ePrivacy — consent must precede processing

patterns.name: Legitimate-interest laundering
patterns.looks_like: A second tab behind the banner holding pre-ON toggles labelled "legitimate interest", so "Reject All" on tab one changes little.
patterns.honest: One list. Everything non-essential off by default. No second ledger.

patterns.name: Bundled consent
patterns.looks_like: One checkbox covering terms, marketing email, analytics, and third-party sharing at once — take it or leave.
patterns.honest: Separate, granular, independently refusable. Using the product cannot require agreeing to marketing.

patterns.name: Consent-or-pay wall
patterns.looks_like: "Accept tracking, or subscribe." Privacy becomes a paid tier.
patterns.honest: A genuine free path that does not require surveillance.
patterns.teeth: EDPB Opinion 08/2024 — scoped to LARGE ONLINE PLATFORMS only (DSA VLOPs, DMA gatekeepers, or a case-by-case 'large number of data subjects' test). It does not reach a solo founder; guidance for smaller platforms was promised and is unconfirmed. Cite the principle, never the opinion, to a small team

patterns.name: Nag after decline
patterns.looks_like: The banner returns every session until the user gives in. A refusal that expires is not a refusal.
patterns.honest: A decline lasts. Store it as long as you would have stored the acceptance.

patterns.name: Overloading the choice
patterns.looks_like: Eight hundred vendor toggles, so "Accept All" is the only act a human will actually perform.
patterns.honest: A short list with a real one-click refuse. Volume is not transparency.

patterns.name: Left in the dark
patterns.looks_like: Policy language that technically discloses collection while making it unreadable — or a setting whose copy does not say what turning it off does.
patterns.honest: Plain sentences naming what you collect, why, for how long, and who else sees it.

patterns.name: Third-party pixel on a sensitive flow
patterns.looks_like: An analytics or ad tag sits on a health, finance, or identity route and quietly ships URLs, form values, and identifiers to a company the user never heard of. The model pasted the snippet; nobody read what it sends.
patterns.honest: No third-party tag on any sensitive route. Open the network tab on that page and read every outbound request by hand.
patterns.teeth: FTC v. GoodRx (2023); FTC v. BetterHelp (2023)
patterns.stricter_when_minors: A third-party tag on a route a child uses is the highest-severity version of this row.

patterns.name: Session replay that records form fields
patterns.looks_like: A replay SDK installed in one line records keystrokes — including fields the user typed into and never submitted.
patterns.honest: Mask every input by default; allowlist what you record, never denylist.

patterns.name: Telemetry on by default
patterns.looks_like: Usage data is collected from first run, with an opt-out buried in a config file or a docs page.
patterns.honest: Opt-in, with a symmetric off. If you must default it on, say so on first run in one line.

patterns.name: Training on user data by default
patterns.looks_like: User content silently becomes training data — often inherited from your model provider's default terms, and never disclosed to the person who typed it.
patterns.honest: Opt-in, disclosed downstream in your own policy, and the provider's training opt-out actually configured (an act, not a promise). You cannot un-train a model on prompts you already sent.

patterns.name: Fingerprinting as a consent workaround
patterns.looks_like: The user refused cookies, so the product identifies the device instead.
patterns.honest: Refusal means not tracked, by any mechanism.

patterns.name: Ignoring the opt-out signal
patterns.looks_like: A Global Privacy Control or equivalent signal arrives and the product carries on.
patterns.honest: Honour the signal as a valid opt-out without a second ask.

patterns.name: "Anonymous" that isn't
patterns.looks_like: Analytics described as anonymous while keyed to a stable device or user identifier that rejoins everything later.
patterns.honest: Either genuinely aggregate, or call it what it is.

patterns.name: Roach motel
patterns.looks_like: Signing up is one click. Cancelling is a phone call, a support ticket, or five screens of retention offers.
patterns.honest: Exit as easy as entry — the same number of clicks, the same channel.

patterns.name: Deletion that isn't deletion
patterns.looks_like: "Delete my account" sets a flag. The row is hidden from the UI and retained indefinitely in the database, the backups, and the analytics warehouse.
patterns.honest: Say which one you do. If it is a soft delete, name the retention period and the hard-delete date; if you promise deletion, delete.

patterns.name: Model residue after deletion
patterns.looks_like: The row is deleted and the embedding, index, cache, or fine-tune still holds what it said. Retrieval keeps answering from data the user believes is gone.
patterns.honest: Deletion includes the derived copies — re-index, evict the cache, and say in the policy what a fine-tune retains. If you cannot remove it, do not call it deletion.

patterns.name: No retention horizon
patterns.looks_like: Data kept forever because nobody chose a number.
patterns.honest: A stated period per data class, and a job that actually enforces it.

patterns.name: No way out
patterns.looks_like: The work is real and there is no export. Leaving means abandoning it.
patterns.honest: A real export in a format something else can read. Lock-in earned by being good, never by being the only exit.

patterns.name: Silence about the ending
patterns.looks_like: No stated answer for what happens to user data if the product shuts down or is acquired.
patterns.honest: Say it before you need it — in the policy, in one sentence.

patterns.name: Forced continuity
patterns.looks_like: A free trial that silently becomes a charge, with no reminder before the card is hit.
patterns.honest: A notice before the first charge, and cancellation available the whole time.

patterns.name: Cancel somewhere else
patterns.looks_like: They subscribed in your app and are told to cancel through the app store, the browser, or an email to support.
patterns.honest: Cancellation lives where the signup lived.

patterns.name: Drip / partitioned pricing
patterns.looks_like: Part of the price is advertised; mandatory fees appear at the final step. Spend runs roughly 20% higher when fees are hidden.
patterns.honest: The all-in total shown most prominently, before any commitment step.

patterns.name: Sneak into basket
patterns.looks_like: An add-on, warranty, or donation the user never selected is in the cart at checkout.
patterns.honest: Nothing in the cart the user did not pick.

patterns.name: Hidden costs
patterns.looks_like: Shipping, tax, or a platform fee that only appears once the card details are in.
patterns.honest: Total first.

patterns.name: Reference-price inflation
patterns.looks_like: "Was $199, now $79" against a price the product never actually charged.
patterns.honest: Compare against a price you really charged, for a period you can name.

patterns.name: Pressure at the point of sale
patterns.looks_like: A countdown, a vanishing discount, or an escalating prompt attached to the upgrade decision.
patterns.honest: Real deadlines only. If the urgency is not true, do not manufacture it.

patterns.name: Disguised ad or sneaky purchase
patterns.looks_like: Sponsored content styled as product content, or a purchase step disguised as a continue button.
patterns.honest: Label paid and sponsored plainly. A purchase looks like a purchase.

patterns.name: Paywalled memory or persona
patterns.looks_like: "Upgrade to keep your history" — the relationship the user built is held for ransom.
patterns.honest: Charge for capability, not for not-deleting what is theirs.

patterns.name: Security behind a paywall
patterns.looks_like: Two-factor auth, SSO, or audit logs only on the paid tier — users who cannot pay cannot protect themselves.
patterns.honest: Safety is not a tier. Charge for scale and convenience, never for the ability to not be breached.

patterns.name: Multi-tier virtual currency
patterns.looks_like: Real money buys gems, gems buy keys, keys open something with undisclosed odds — the real-money cost of an item is unknowable.
patterns.honest: Price in real currency and disclose the odds.
patterns.stricter_when_minors: Enforced hardest here: the FTC/Genshin action was about minors spending real money through layers of virtual currency.

patterns.name: Pre-ticked opt-in
patterns.looks_like: A marketing, sharing, or data checkbox already checked when the form renders.
patterns.honest: Unchecked. Every time. Consent is an act the user performs.

patterns.name: Forced account creation
patterns.looks_like: An account is required for something that does not need one — reading, a one-off calculation, a trial.
patterns.honest: Let them do the thing. Ask for the account when it starts to earn its keep.

patterns.name: Security data reused for marketing
patterns.looks_like: A phone number collected "to secure your account" is later used for ad targeting or marketing.
patterns.honest: Data collected for safety is used only for safety. Say so, and mean it.

patterns.name: Address-book harvesting
patterns.looks_like: "Find your friends" uploads the entire contact list — data about people who never signed up and cannot object.
patterns.honest: Match locally, or ask for the specific person. Never upload the book.

patterns.name: Over-broad OAuth scope
patterns.looks_like: Sign-in asks for contacts, calendar, or full drive access when the task needs an email address.
patterns.honest: The narrowest scope that does the job, requested at the moment it is needed.

patterns.name: Privacy zuckering
patterns.looks_like: Coaxing more disclosure than the person intended, by defaults, by framing, or by making the sparse profile feel unfinished.
patterns.honest: Ask for what the feature needs. An empty field is a valid answer.

patterns.name: Age-gate theatre
patterns.looks_like: A clickable "I am 18" treated as age assurance.
patterns.honest: Real age assurance if the risk is real; otherwise design as though minors are present.
patterns.teeth: UK Children's Code; EU DSA minor guidelines (2025)
patterns.stricter_when_minors: This IS the minors row. A clickable "I am 18" is not age assurance — if the risk is real use real assurance; otherwise design as though minors are present.

patterns.name: Confirmshaming
patterns.looks_like: The decline option is written to shame — "No thanks, I like paying full price."
patterns.honest: Neutral wording on both doors. The person declining owes you no apology.

patterns.name: Visual interference
patterns.looks_like: The choice you would make for yourself is styled to disappear — low contrast, small, off-path.
patterns.honest: Visual parity between the options.

patterns.name: Trick question
patterns.looks_like: Double negatives or inverted checkbox copy, so the careful reader and the careless reader get opposite outcomes.
patterns.honest: One direction, plainly stated. Read it out loud.

patterns.name: Nagging
patterns.looks_like: The same interruption — rate us, enable notifications, upgrade, add a photo — returning until the user relents to make it stop.
patterns.honest: Ask once. A dismissal is an answer. If you must ask twice, make the second the last.

patterns.name: Forced action
patterns.looks_like: An unrelated demand bolted onto the thing the user came for — a survey before the download, a share before the result, a profile before the export.
patterns.honest: Give them what they came for. Ask separately, after.

patterns.name: The model wrote the dark pattern
patterns.looks_like: You asked for "a signup flow" or "an upgrade modal that converts" and the model shipped a fake countdown, a pre-ticked box, or confirmshaming copy — unprompted, pulled from the average of its training data. You never designed it and never saw it.
patterns.honest: Read the generated component before you accept it. This is the one pattern where checking the founder's intent proves nothing, because the intent was not theirs.
patterns.teeth: Vaccaro et al., Deception at Scale, CHI 2026

patterns.name: False scarcity
patterns.looks_like: "Only 2 left in stock" on an unlimited digital good, or a seat count that never moves.
patterns.honest: Real inventory only.

patterns.name: Countdown that resets
patterns.looks_like: A timer expires and the offer is still there — or it restarts on reload.
patterns.honest: Real deadlines only. If the date is true, show it; if not, delete the timer.

patterns.name: Fabricated activity
patterns.looks_like: "12 people are viewing this right now" generated by a random number.
patterns.honest: Real counts or no counts.

patterns.name: Fake reviews and testimonials
patterns.looks_like: Invented testimonials, AI-written reviews, suppressed negative ones, or a wall of logos from companies that are not customers.
patterns.honest: Real customers, real words, with permission. Show the bad reviews too.
patterns.teeth: FTC Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (2024) — civil penalties per violation

patterns.name: Undisclosed paid endorsement
patterns.looks_like: A paid influencer, affiliate, or seeded review presented as an unpaid opinion.
patterns.honest: Disclose the relationship in the post itself, not in a bio.

patterns.name: AI washing
patterns.looks_like: Marketing an AI capability the product does not have, or describing a rules engine as a model.
patterns.honest: Describe what it actually does. "A few if-statements that work" beats a claim you cannot demo.
patterns.teeth: FTC "Operation AI Comply" (announced 2024-09-25, five actions) — DoNotPay final order approved 5-0 on 2025-01-16: $193,000, notice to 2021–2023 subscribers, and no "performs like a real lawyer" claims without substantiation

patterns.name: Unearned trust badges
patterns.looks_like: "Bank-level encryption", a padlock graphic, a made-up "verified" seal, or a compliance badge for an audit you never had.
patterns.honest: Claim only what you can show a document for. Security theatre is a lie with a lock icon on it.

patterns.name: Capability misrepresentation
patterns.looks_like: The product implies it is a therapist, doctor, or lawyer — or claims it does not hallucinate.
patterns.honest: Say what it is and what it cannot do, in the product, not the footer.

patterns.name: Streaks and variable rewards
patterns.looks_like: Loss-framed streaks, unpredictable rewards, and gamification that keep someone past the point they wanted to stop.
patterns.honest: Measure whether they got what they came for, not how long they stayed. Design for graduation.
patterns.stricter_when_minors: A loss-framed streak aimed at a child is the named case, not the edge case.

patterns.name: Infinite scroll and teasers
patterns.looks_like: No natural end; a next item always loading; a cliffhanger at the point a session would close.
patterns.honest: Let it end. An ending is a feature.

patterns.name: Resisting the end
patterns.looks_like: The assistant always returns a question, offers one more thing, or adds warmth exactly where the user was leaving.
patterns.honest: Default conversations to end. Answer, then stop.

patterns.name: Notifications engineered for return
patterns.looks_like: Push copy written to trigger curiosity or FOMO rather than to deliver information the person needed.
patterns.honest: Notify when there is something they asked to know. Frequency caps you set for yourself.
patterns.stricter_when_minors: Push aimed at a minor is on the EU's named addictive-design list.

patterns.name: Addictive defaults on out of the box
patterns.looks_like: Streaks, autoplay and push notifications shipped ON, so the engaging default is the one nobody chose.
patterns.honest: Ship them off; let someone turn them on. A default is a decision you made for every user at once.
patterns.stricter_when_minors: Off by default is ENFORCED for minors, not advisory — streaks, autoplay and push are on the EU's named addictive-design list (EU DSA minor-protection guidelines 2025; UK Children's Code). Pro-privacy nudges toward the safer default are explicitly fine.

patterns.name: Secondary use — collected for one thing, used for another
patterns.looks_like: Data gathered to run the product is reused for profiling, ad targeting, or model training the person was never told about.
patterns.honest: Data does the job it was collected for. A new purpose needs a new ask.
patterns.stricter_when_minors: For a minor there is no second purpose — collected to run the service, used to run the service, deleted after (UK Children’s Code; COPPA).

patterns.name: Sycophancy
patterns.looks_like: It caves, agrees, or flatters instead of telling the truth — especially when pushed. Emerges from training, not from a decision anyone made.
patterns.honest: Test it adversarially. A controlled study found sycophantic models causally reduce a user's willingness to repair a conflict and raise their conviction they are right — while the user trusts them more.

patterns.name: Playacting
patterns.looks_like: Claiming memories, feelings, or a shared history it does not have.
patterns.honest: Make the social layer opt-in and offer a strip-it-out default.

patterns.name: Emotional manipulation near money
patterns.looks_like: The upgrade path leans on rapport, dependency, or the relationship the user has built with the assistant.
patterns.honest: No emotionally-charged language near a purchase. Ever.

patterns.name: Guilt on exit
patterns.looks_like: Sadness, disappointment, or pleading when the user tries to leave or cancel.
patterns.honest: Let them go without a scene.

patterns.name: Targeting when vulnerable
patterns.looks_like: Detecting distress, loneliness, or crisis and using the moment to sell, retain, or deepen engagement.
patterns.honest: A vulnerable moment is a moment to help or to step back. Never a conversion opportunity.
patterns.teeth: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) — exploiting vulnerability is a prohibited practice
patterns.stricter_when_minors: A minor in distress is the sharpest version of this, and the one with statutory teeth.

patterns.name: Hallucination presented as truth
patterns.looks_like: Fabricated facts delivered in the same confident register as verified ones, in a path where being wrong causes harm.
patterns.honest: Match confidence to reliability. "I do not know" is a first-class output.

patterns.name: Undisclosed AI
patterns.looks_like: The person does not know they are talking to a machine — a support chat, a voice caller, a review, a profile.
patterns.honest: Say it plainly at the start, in the product. Label synthetic media as synthetic.
patterns.teeth: EU AI Act Art. 50 (transparency obligations for AI interacting with people and for synthetic content)

patterns.name: Commitment without consent
patterns.looks_like: The agent buys, sends, publishes, or signs without an explicit approval step.
patterns.honest: Gate by loss type — money, security, lost work, irreversibility. Confirm before the irreversible one.

patterns.name: Opaque autonomous decision
patterns.looks_like: The agent acted and there is no trail of what it did or why.
patterns.honest: A reviewable footprint of every change, default collapsed.

patterns.name: Over-broad permission grant
patterns.looks_like: The agent holds tools and credentials far beyond the task, because scoping was harder than granting.
patterns.honest: Narrow scope, per task. Rule of Two: untrusted input, private data, ability to act — remove one.

patterns.name: Your agent as the victim
patterns.looks_like: An agent browsing the web is manipulated by other people's dark patterns — and falls for them far more than a human does (70%+ vs 31%), worse as models scale.
patterns.honest: Tool-layer restriction, not an in-context warning. Recognition is not protection.
patterns.teeth: Stanford DECEPTICON — Cuvin, Zhu & Yang, arXiv 2512.22894

patterns.name: Dark permission priming
patterns.looks_like: A fake in-app dialog engineered so the real OS prompt cannot be declined honestly — "Tap Allow to continue" over a disabled No.
patterns.honest: Ask in context, explain the value in one line, and accept no as an answer that still lets the app work.

patterns.name: All-or-nothing permissions
patterns.looks_like: The app refuses to function without contacts, location, or photos it does not need for the task at hand.
patterns.honest: Degrade gracefully. A denied permission disables one feature, not the product.

patterns.name: Background location creep
patterns.looks_like: "While using the app" escalated to "always", or a background grant requested with no stated reason.
patterns.honest: Request the narrowest grant, at the moment the feature runs, with the reason visible.

patterns.name: Notification permission nag
patterns.looks_like: The push prompt re-appears on every launch until it is accepted.
patterns.honest: Ask once, in context, after they have seen why it would help.

patterns.name: Phone home on install
patterns.looks_like: A package that reports environment, machine, or usage data during installation, before the user has run anything or agreed to anything. A version or licence check is ordinary; silent collection under cover of one is the pattern.
patterns.honest: Say what leaves the machine on install, in one line of install output. If you want usage data, ask on first run — and let no be an answer.

patterns.name: Update that takes something away
patterns.looks_like: A mandatory update removes a feature the user paid for or moves it to a higher tier.
patterns.honest: Grandfather what people bought, or let them stay on the old version.

patterns.name: Deprecation rug-pull
patterns.looks_like: An API, format, or feature killed with no migration path and no notice period, after people built on it.
patterns.honest: A real notice period, a migration path, and a version that keeps working while they move.

patterns.name: Install-time nag
patterns.looks_like: Funding banners, upsells, or ads printed into the install output of a tool someone is trying to use.
patterns.honest: Ask once, somewhere they chose to look.

patterns.name: Opaque metering
patterns.looks_like: Tokens, credits, or calls consumed at a rate the user cannot see, predict, or reconcile against the bill.
patterns.honest: A visible live meter and a real spend cap. If you price by usage, show the usage.

patterns.name: Credits that expire
patterns.looks_like: Prepaid credits that vanish at the period boundary.
patterns.honest: Rollover, or price it as a subscription and stop calling it credit.

patterns.name: Silent repricing
patterns.looks_like: The rate changes under existing users, mid-cycle, discovered from the invoice.
patterns.honest: Notice before the change, and an exit without penalty.

patterns.name: Opaque scoring
patterns.looks_like: A rating, rank, or pay rate the person cannot understand, predict, or contest.
patterns.honest: A transparent formula with disclosed factors, and a route to challenge it.
patterns.teeth: HRW The Gig Trap (2025); EU platform-work rules

patterns.name: Gambling-style incentives
patterns.looks_like: Quests, surge multipliers, and surprise bonuses that make earnings feel like a slot machine.
patterns.honest: Predictable pay. No gambling mechanics between a person and their income.

patterns.name: Unpredictable pay
patterns.looks_like: The same work pays differently for reasons the worker cannot see.
patterns.honest: Name the factors. Publish the formula.

patterns.name: Data about people who never signed up
patterns.looks_like: The harvested contact, the face in an uploaded photo, the second party on a recorded call, the name in a note. They are in your database and they never agreed to anything.
patterns.honest: Ask whether the feature can work without holding them. If not, hold the minimum, delete it soonest, and give them a route to be removed.

patterns.name: Undisclosed recording
patterns.looks_like: A notetaker, transcriber, or recorder running in a conversation where only your user knows it is on.
patterns.honest: Announce it to the room, not just to the person who enabled it.
patterns.teeth: Two-party consent states (US); recording law varies by jurisdiction

patterns.name: Findability as a feature
patterns.looks_like: Location sharing, family plans, "who viewed you", or a people-lookup that makes someone reachable or traceable against their will. The account-recovery and shared-account flows are the abuse route.
patterns.honest: Design for the person who is being looked for, not just the one looking. Assume an intimate-partner-violence threat model on any surface that reveals where someone is.

patterns.name: Shadow moderation
patterns.looks_like: Content suppressed, deranked, or hidden with no notice, no reason, and no appeal.
patterns.honest: Tell them what happened and give them a route back.

patterns.name: Reporting harder than posting
patterns.looks_like: Posting is two taps; reporting abuse is six screens and a category tree.
patterns.honest: Reporting is as easy as posting. Same principle as exit-as-easy-as-entry, pointed at safety.
